claim: Tumorigenesis is driven by the joint actions of many mutations.
source: Tumorigenesis, like most complex genetic traits, is driven by the joint actions of many mutations.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The full sets of CDNs are necessary for understanding and treating each cancer patient.
source: The full sets of CDNs are necessary, and perhaps even sufficient, for the understanding and treatment of each cancer patient.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' theoretical framework and reasoning about cancer treatment.

claim: Currently, only a small fraction of CDNs is known because most mutations in tumors are not drivers.
source: Currently, only a small fraction of CDNs is known as most mutations accrued in tumors are not drivers.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field based on current understanding.

claim: Cancer evolution is massively repeated in millions of individuals.
source: We now develop the theory of CDNs on the basis that cancer evolution is massively repeated in millions of individuals.
evidence: This is a foundational assumption of the theoretical framework presented.

claim: Any advantageous mutation should recur frequently in cancer evolution.
source: Hence, any advantageous mutation should recur frequently and, conversely, any mutation that does not is either a passenger or deleterious mutation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the theory of massively repeated evolution.

claim: No neutral mutation can reach i*=3 recurrences in the TCGA database.
source: Since no neutral mutation can reach i*=3, all mutations recurring at i≥3 are CDNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion derived from the mathematical modeling presented in the study.

claim: All mutations recurring at i≥3 are CDNs.
source: Since no neutral mutation can reach i*=3, all mutations recurring at i≥3 are CDNs.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion from the theoretical model and data analysis.

claim: The theory shows the feasibility of identifying almost all CDNs if n increases to 100,000 for each cancer type.
source: The theory shows the feasibility of identifying almost all CDNs if n increases to 100,000 for each cancer type.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the mathematical modeling and extrapolation to larger sample sizes.

claim: At present, only <10% of CDNs have been identified.
source: At present, only <10% of CDNs have been identified.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the current analysis of available data.

claim: Cancer hallmarks include sustaining growth signaling, evading growth suppression, resisting apoptosis, achieving immortality, and executing metastasis.
source: The ensemble has been characterized as 'cancer hallmarks' that include sustaining growth signaling, evading growth suppression, resisting apoptosis, achieving immortality, executing metastasis and so on Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Hanahan, 2022.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on cancer hallmarks.

claim: Each of the 6–10 cancer hallmarks is governed by a set of mutations.
source: It seems likely that each of the 6–10 cancer hallmarks is governed by a set of mutations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the authors' interpretation of cancer biology.

claim: Most, if not all, cancer-driving mutations are jointly needed to drive tumorigenesis.
source: Most, if not all, of these mutations are jointly needed to drive the tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on the multi-hit model of cancer.

claim: Cancers do not differ fundamentally from other complex traits whereby multiple mutations are simultaneously needed.
source: In the genetic sense, cancers do not differ fundamentally from other complex traits whereby multiple mutations are simultaneously needed to execute the program.
evidence: This is a conceptual claim drawing parallels between cancer and other genetic phenomena.

claim: The early onset of COVID-19 requires all four mutations of the D614G group.
source: The early onset of COVID-19 requires all four mutations of the D614G group and the later Delta strain has 31 mutations accrued in three batches (Ruan et al., 2022b; Ruan et al., 2022a; Cao et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies on SARS-CoV-2 evolution.

claim: The Delta strain of SARS-CoV-2 has 31 mutations accrued in three batches.
source: The early onset of COVID-19 requires all four mutations of the D614G group and the later Delta strain has 31 mutations accrued in three batches (Ruan et al., 2022b; Ruan et al., 2022a; Cao et al., 2023; Ruan et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies on SARS-CoV-2 evolution.

claim: Each cancer mutation has been shown to be insufficient for tumorigenesis until many are co-introduced.
source: While cancer research has often proceeded one mutation at a time, each of the mutations has been shown to be insufficient for tumorigenesis until many (Ortmann et al., 2015; Takeda, 2021; Hodis et al., 2022) are co-introduced.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The number of key cancer drivers has been variously estimated to be 6–10.
source: The number of key drivers has been variously estimated to be 6–10 (Martincorena et al., 2017; Anandakrishnan et al., 2019; ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies estimating driver numbers.

claim: Cancer driving point mutations (CDNs) are abundant.
source: Although cancer driving 'point mutations', referred to as Cancer Driving Nucleotides (or CDNs), are not the only drivers, they are indeed abundant (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a large-scale cancer genomics study.

claim: CDNs may be the only type of drivers that can be fully identified.
source: Furthermore, CDNs, being easily quantifiable, may be the only type of drivers that can be fully identified (see below).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the quantifiable nature of point mutations.

claim: This study focuses on clonal mutations present in all cells of the tumor without considering within-tumor heterogeneity.
source: Here, we will focus on the clonal mutations present in all cells of the tumor without considering within-tumor heterogeneity for now (Ling et al., 2015; Turajlic et al., 2019; Black and McGranahan, 2021; Chen et al., 2022a; Zhai et al., 2022; Bian et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a methodological choice stated explicitly with supporting citations.

claim: Somatic evolution proceeds in parallel in millions of humans.
source: Since somatic evolution proceeds in parallel in millions of humans, point mutations can recur multiple times as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a foundational premise of the study's theoretical framework.

claim: Point mutations can recur multiple times in cancer evolution.
source: Since somatic evolution proceeds in parallel in millions of humans, point mutations can recur multiple times as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated both in the text and in Figure 1.

claim: Recurrences of mutations permit the detection of advantageous mutations with unprecedented power.
source: The recurrences should permit the detection of advantageous mutations with unprecedented power.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the power of the recurrence-based approach.

claim: Mutations that do not recur frequently are unlikely to be advantageous.
source: The converse should also be true that mutations that do not recur frequently are unlikely to be advantageous.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the theory of recurrent mutations.

claim: In cancer evolution, the same mutation at the same site may occasionally be seen in multiple sequences.
source: In cancer evolution, the same mutation at the same site may occasionally be seen in multiple sequences.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about cancer mutation patterns, illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Hotspots of recurrent mutations have been commonly reported in the literature.
source: In the literature, hotspots of recurrent mutations have been commonly reported (Gartner et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016; Cannataro et al., 2018; Buisson et al., 2019; Hess et al., 2019; Stobbe et al., 2019; Juul et al., 2021; Nesta et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Bergstrom et al., 2022; Sherman et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2022; Zeng and Bromberg, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to the literature.

claim: A hotspot could be either a mutational or functional hotspot.
source: A hotspot, however, could be either a mutational or functional hotspot.
evidence: This is a conceptual distinction made by the authors.

claim: Mutational hotspots are properties of the mutation machinery that include nucleotide composition, local chromatin structure, and timing of replication.
source: Mutational hotspots are the properties of the mutation machinery that would include nucleotide composition, local chromatin structure, timing of replication, etc. (Stamatoyannopoulos et al., 2009; Pleasance et al., 2010; Makova and Hardison, 2015; Polak et al., 2015; Martincorena et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mutation mechanisms.

claim: Functional hotspots are CDNs under positive selection.
source: In contrast, functional hotspots are CDNs under positive selection.
evidence: This is a definitional statement distinguishing functional from mutational hotspots.

claim: CDN evolution is akin to convergent evolution that repeats itself in different taxa.
source: CDN evolution is akin to 'convergent evolution' that repeats itself in different taxa (He et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020b; Wu et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2022b; Wu, 2023) and is generally considered the most convincing proof of positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on convergent evolution.

claim: Convergent evolution is generally considered the most convincing proof of positive selection.
source: CDN evolution is akin to 'convergent evolution' that repeats itself in different taxa (He et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020b; Wu et al., 2020; Pan et al., 2022b; Wu, 2023) and is generally considered the most convincing proof of positive selection.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of convergent evolution in evolutionary biology.

claim: Many studies conclude that sites of mutation recurrence are largely mutational hotspots.
source: While many studies conclude that sites of mutation recurrence are largely mutational hotspots (Buisson et al., 2019; Hess et al., 2019; Stobbe et al., 2019; Nesta et al., 2021; Bergstrom et al., 2022), others deem them functional hotspots, driven by positive selection (Gartner et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016; Bailey et al., 2018; Cannataro et al., 2018; Juul et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Zeng and Bromberg, 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Other studies deem recurrent mutation sites as functional hotspots driven by positive selection.
source: While many studies conclude that sites of mutation recurrence are largely mutational hotspots (Buisson et al., 2019; Hess et al., 2019; Stobbe et al., 2019; Nesta et al., 2021; Bergstrom et al., 2022), others deem them functional hotspots, driven by positive selection (Gartner et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2016; Bailey et al., 2018; Cannataro et al., 2018; Juul et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Zeng and Bromberg, 2022).
evidence: This is a summary of the literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies make assumptions about the relative importance of mutation and selection mechanisms when extracting information from the same data.
source: In the attempt to distinguish between these two hypotheses, studies make assumptions, often implicitly, about the relative importance of the two mechanisms in their estimation procedures. The conclusions naturally manifest the assumptions made when extracting information on mutation and selection from the same data (Elliott and Larsson, 2021).
evidence: This is a critical observation about methodological issues in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The study analyzes mutational characteristics of sequences surrounding CDNs.
source: First, the mutational characteristics of sequences surrounding CDNs are analyzed.
evidence: This describes the first part of the study's methodology.

claim: A rigorous probability model is developed to compute the recurrence level at any sample size.
source: Second, a rigorous probability model is developed to compute the recurrence level at any sample size.
evidence: This describes the second part of the study's methodology.

claim: Above a threshold of recurrence, all mutations are CDNs.
source: Above a threshold of recurrence, all mutations are CDNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the probability model developed in the study.

claim: The study determines the necessary sample sizes that will yield most, if not all, CDNs.
source: Third, we determine the necessary sample sizes that will yield most, if not all, CDNs.
evidence: This describes the third part of the study's methodology.

claim: The TCGA database is used because it is well established and covers the entire coding region.
source: The TCGA database is used as it is well established and covers the entire coding region (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological choice explained with a citation.

claim: In lung cancer (n=1035), there are approximately 0.2 million sites with one hit (A1=195,958).
source: There are 22.5 million nonsynonymous sites, among which ~0.2 million sites have one hit (A1=195,958) in 1035 patients.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Table 1.

claim: In lung cancer, the number of recurrent mutation sites decreases sharply as i increases.
source: The number then decreases sharply as i increases. Thus, A2=2946 (number of 2-hit sites), A3=99, and A4 +A5 +...=79.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Table 1.

claim: In lung cancer, the Ai/Si ratio increases from 2.89, 2.82, 3.04 to 4.71 as i increases.
source: We also note that the Ai/Si ratio increases from 2.89, 2.82, 3.04–4.71 and so on.
evidence: This is a direct report of data from Table 1.

claim: The average of Ai and Si among the 12 cancer types shows that A1 and S1 decrease to ~0.002 of A0 and S0.
source: In the actual data, (A1) and S1 decrease to ~0.002 of A0 and S0, the step being least affected by selection (see PART II later).
evidence: This is a report of data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: For A2 and S2, the decrease is only ~0.01 of A1 and S1.
source: For A2 and S2, the decrease is only ~0.01 of A1 and S1.
evidence: This is a report of data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The decrease from i to i+1 becomes smaller and smaller as i increases, suggesting that the process is not entirely neutral.
source: The decrease from i to i+1 becomes smaller and smaller as i increases, suggesting that the process in not entirely neutral.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern observed in Figure 2.

claim: The Ai/Si ratio continues to rise as i increases, suggesting stronger positive selection at higher i values.
source: Furthermore, the lower panel of Figure 2 shows that Ai/Si continues to rise as i increases. These patterns again suggest a stronger positive selection at higher i values.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data pattern shown in Figure 2.

claim: The extrapolation lines in Figure 2 roughly define i=3 as a cutoff where the expected (A3) falls below 1.
source: The extrapolation lines shown in Figure 2 roughly define i=3 as a cutoff where the expected (A3) falls below 1 (see PART II for details).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the visual analysis of Figure 2.

claim: High recurrence sites (i≥3) are defined as CDNs by the precise model.
source: The precise model of PART II will define high recurrence sites (i≥3) as CDNs.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's definition of CDNs.

claim: CpG sites account for ~6.5% of the coding sequences but contribute ~22% among the mutated sites.
source: Indeed, CpG sites account for ~6.5% of the coding sequences but contributing ~22% among the mutated sites in Figure 2.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about CpG site contribution to mutations.

claim: In mammals, methylation and de-amination enhance the mutation rate from CpG to TpG or CpA by five- to tenfold.
source: In mammals, methylation and de-amination would enhance the mutation rate from CpG to TpG or CpA by five-~tenfold (Hodgkinson and Eyre-Walker, 2011; Ségurel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CpG mutation mechanisms.

claim: The sevenfold increase in the CpG mutation rate contributes more to Ai and Si as i increases.
source: Hence, the sevenfold increase in the CpG mutation rate should contribute more to Ai and Si as i increases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of CpG sites.

claim: Even with a 10-fold increase in mutation rate, the decrease rate would still be 0.02.
source: Thus, even with a 10-fold increase in mutation rate, the decrease rate would still be 0.02.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the theoretical model.

claim: The mutation rate of each nucleotide (u) follows a Gamma distribution with a scale parameter θ and a shape parameter k.
source: The mutation rate of each nucleotide (u) follows a Gamma distribution with a scale parameter θ and a shape parameter k.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated explicitly.

claim: The Gamma distribution has a long tail suited to modeling a small number of sites with very high mutation rate.
source: In particular, the Gamma distribution has a long tail suited to modeling a small number of sites with very high mutation rate.
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of distribution in the model.

claim: E(u) is generally (1~5)×10^-6 per site in cancer genomic data.
source: E(u) of Equations 2 and 3 is generally (1~5)×10–6 per site in cancer genomic data and n is generally between 300 and 1000.
evidence: This is a statement about the typical mutation rate observed in cancer data.

claim: In the TCGA data, n is generally between 300 and 1000.
source: E(u) of Equations 2 and 3 is generally (1~5)×10–6 per site in cancer genomic data and n is generally between 300 and 1000.
evidence: This is a statement about the sample sizes in the TCGA database.

claim: nE(u) is generally between 0.001 and 0.005 in the TCGA data.
source: Hence, nE(u) is the total mutation rate summed over all n patients and is generally between 0.001 and 0.005 in the TCGA data.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the mutation rate and sample size.

claim: Given nE(u) is in the order of 10^-3, Si and Ai would both decrease by 2~3 orders of magnitude with each increment of i by 1.
source: Given nE(u) is in the order of 10–3, Si and Ai would both decrease by 2~3 orders of magnitude with each increment of i by 1.
evidence: This is a mathematical consequence of the model.

claim: The total number of synonymous sites, LS, is ~0.9 × 10^7.
source: We note that the total number of synonymous sites, LS, is ~0.9 × 107 and LA is ~2.3 times larger.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic composition of coding regions.

claim: LA is ~2.3 times larger than LS.
source: We note that the total number of synonymous sites, LS, is ~0.9 × 107 and LA is ~2.3 times larger.
evidence: This is a statement about the genomic composition of coding regions.

claim: S3 <1 and A3 <1 for each cancer type.
source: Therefore, S3 <1 and A3 <1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model.

claim: When i reaches 4, Si ≥4 and Ai ≥4 would both be ≪ 1 when averaged over cancer types.
source: When i reaches 4, Si ≥4 and Ai ≥4 would both be ≪ 1 when averaged over cancer types.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model.

claim: With n<1000, neutral mutations are unlikely to recur 3 times or more in the TCGA data (i*=3).
source: In other words, with n<1000,, neutral mutations are unlikely to recur 3 times or more in the TCGA data (i*=3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mathematical model applied to the TCGA data.

claim: When n reaches 10,000, i* will be 6.
source: At n≤1,000 for the TCGA data, i* should be 3 but, when n reaches 10,000, i* will be 6.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model for larger sample sizes.

claim: The study assumes a small fraction of sites (p) to be hyper-mutable that is α fold more mutable than the genomic mean.
source: We therefore expand the model by assuming a small fraction of sites (p) to be hyper-mutable that is α fold more mutable than the genomic mean.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption to account for potential outliers.

claim: α and p are likely the inverse of each other.
source: Most likely, α and p are the inverse of each other.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relationship between the two parameters.

claim: Even with the purely conjectured existence of outliers in mutation rate, i*=4 is already too high a cutoff.
source: Hence, even with the purely conjectured existence of outliers in mutation rate, i*=4 is already too high a cutoff.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the outlier model analysis presented in Table 2.

claim: Although mutational bias alone cannot account for the high occurrences, selection can easily do so.
source: We now show that, although the mutational bias alone cannot account for the high occurrences, selection can easily do so.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the mutational and selection models.

claim: CpG sites (many of which fall in functional sites) are expected to be strongly represented among high recurrence sites.
source: Equation 4 also shows that w and E(u) jointly affect the recurrence; therefore, CpG sites (many of which fall in functional sites) are expected to be strongly represented among high recurrence sites.
evidence: This is a prediction from the selection model.

claim: Each sequenced cancer genome in the current databases, on average, harbors only 1~2 CDNs.
source: Using the theory of CDN developed above, the companion paper shows that each sequenced cancer genome in the current databases, on average, harbors only 1~2 CDNs.
evidence: This is a finding from the companion study referenced.

claim: Tumorigenesis may require at least 5~10 driver mutations.
source: For comparison, tumorigenesis may require at least 5~10 driver mutations as estimated by various criteria (Armitage and Doll, 1954; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Belikov, 2017; Martincorena et al., 2017; Anandakrishnan et al., 2019; ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies estimating driver numbers.

claim: There are many more CDNs that have not been discovered.
source: The results show that there are many more CDNs that have not been discovered.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the observed CDNs to the estimated total number needed.

claim: Most CDNs are found in <1% of patients.
source: This is not unexpected since most CDNs are found in <1% of patients.
evidence: This is an observation about the prevalence distribution of CDNs.

claim: If each CDN is observed in 1% of patients and each patient has 5 CDNs, then there should be at least 500 CDNs for each cancer type.
source: If each CDN is observed in 1% of patients and each patient has 5 CDNs, then there should be at least 500 CDNs for each cancer type.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the assumptions about CDN prevalence and number per patient.

claim: The estimated number of CDNs ranges from 500 to 2000 using the A/S ratios.
source: In the companion study that uses the A/S ratios of Figure 1, the estimated number of CDNs ranges from 500 to 2000, whereas the current estimates based on Ai ≥3 sites is only 50~100 (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a finding from the companion study referenced.

claim: The current estimates based on Ai ≥3 sites is only 50~100 CDNs.
source: In the companion study that uses the A/S ratios of Figure 1, the estimated number of CDNs ranges from 500 to 2000, whereas the current estimates based on Ai ≥3 sites is only 50~100 (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The bulk of CDNs must be among A1 and A2 sites.
source: Since all Ai ≥3 sites are concluded to be CDNs, the bulk of CDNs must be among A1 and A2 sites.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the discrepancy between observed and estimated CDN numbers.

claim: The best way to identify the CDNs hidden in A1 and A2 is to increase the sample size, n, dramatically.
source: The best way to identify the CDNs hidden in A1 and A2 is to increase the sample size, n, dramatically.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the theoretical analysis.

claim: When n approaches 10^5, the number of CDNs will likely increase more than 10-fold.
source: When n approaches 105, the number of CDNs will likely increase more than 10-fold as conjectured in Figure 7A.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the theoretical model and illustrated in Figure 7A.

claim: When n approaches 10^5, every patient would have approximately 5 CDNs that can be subjected to gene targeting.
source: In that case, every patient would have, say, 5 CDNs that can be subjected to gene targeting.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the expected increase in CDN discovery.

claim: At present, an average cancer patient would have fewer than one targetable CDN.
source: (The companion study shows that, at present, an average cancer patient would have fewer than one targetable CDN.)
evidence: This is a finding from the companion study referenced.

claim: The analysis of CDNs identifies a potential set of 1.6 times more driver genes than those detected by whole gene selection signal calls.
source: In the companion study, we demonstrate that the analysis of CDNs identifies a potential set of 1.6 times more driver genes than those detected by whole gene selection signal calls (Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a finding from the companion study referenced.

claim: The prevalence (i/n) of sites is well correlated between datasets of different n (TCGA with n<1000 and GENIE with generally tenfold higher).
source: (Figure 7B) shows that the i/n ratios indeed correspond well between TCGA and GENIE, which differ by 10–20-fold in sample size.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7B comparing the two databases.

claim: The number of CDNs increases by three to fivefold when comparing GENIE to TCGA.
source: Importantly, as predicted in Figure 6, the number of CDNs increases by three to fivefold (Figure 7C-E).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 7C-E comparing CDN discovery in the two databases.

claim: Many newly discovered CDNs from GENIE are found in the A1 and A2 classes of TCGA.
source: Many of these newly discovered CDNs from GENIE are found in the A1 and A2 classes of TCGA while many more are found in the A0 class in TCGA.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two databases.

claim: Increasing n by one to two orders of magnitude would be the simplest means of finding all CDNs.
source: In conclusion, increasing n by one to two orders of magnitude would be the simplest means of finding all CDNs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis of TCGA and GENIE data.

claim: The nature of high-recurrence mutations has been controversial.
source: The nature of high-recurrence mutations has been controversial.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: The mutational hotspot hypothesis and the selection hypothesis are incompatible.
source: While the two views co-exist, they are in fact incompatible.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the relationship between the two hypotheses.

claim: If the mutational hotspot hypothesis is correct, the selection hypothesis would not be needed.
source: If the mutational hotspot hypothesis is correct, the selection hypothesis, and the determination of CDNs, would not be needed.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the mutational hotspot hypothesis.

claim: This study is the first to comprehensively test the null hypothesis of mutational hotspots.
source: We believe that this study is the first to comprehensively test of the null hypothesis of mutational hotspots.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's approach.

claim: It is possible to reject the null hypothesis of mutational hotspots for recurrences as low as 3 in the TCGA data.
source: The conclusion is that it is possible to reject the null hypothesis for recurrences as low as 3 in the TCGA data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis presented.

claim: The theory developed can help the search for unknown mutation mechanisms, if they do exist.
source: In a sense, the theory developed here can help the search for such unknown mutation mechanisms, if they do exist.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications of the theory.

claim: When n reaches 10^5, any point mutation with a prevalence higher than 12/100,000 would be a CDN.
source: When n reaches 105, any point mutation with a prevalence higher than 12/100,000 would be a CDN, which is 25-fold more sensitive than in the TCGA data (3/1000).
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model for large sample sizes.

claim: The sensitivity at n=10^5 is 25-fold more than in the TCGA data (3/1000).
source: When n reaches 105, any point mutation with a prevalence higher than 12/100,000 would be a CDN, which is 25-fold more sensitive than in the TCGA data (3/1000).
evidence: This is a calculation comparing the sensitivity at different sample sizes.

claim: CDNs with lower prevalence may still be highly tumorigenic in patients with the said mutation.
source: The companion analysis suggests that CDNs with lower prevalence, say 12/100,000 may still be highly tumorigenic in patients with the said mutation.
evidence: This is a finding from the companion study referenced.

claim: Prevalence and potence of CDNs are poorly correlated.
source: If prevalence and potence are indeed poorly correlated, the search for lower prevalence CDNs by increasing n to 105 is equivalent to searching for less common but still potent cancer driving mutations.
evidence: This is a conditional statement based on findings from the companion study.

claim: When we have all CDNs identified, a patient can be expected to have multiple (≥5) CDNs.
source: When we have all CDNs identified, a patient can be expected to have multiple (≥5; Zhang et al., 2024) CDNs.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the companion study referenced.

claim: Targeting multiple mutations simultaneously is necessary and may even be sufficient for cancer treatment.
source: Targeting multiple mutations simultaneously is necessary and may even be sufficient.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications for cancer treatment.

claim: When multiple CDN mutations in the same patient can be simultaneously targeted, the efficacy should be high.
source: When multiple CDN mutations in the same patient can be simultaneously targeted, the efficacy should be high.
evidence: This is a speculation about the benefits of multi-target therapy.

claim: Resistance to treatment should be diminished when targeting multiple CDNs since it would be harder on cancer cells to evolve multiple escape routes.
source: No less crucial, resistance to treatment should be diminished since it would be harder on cancer cells to evolve multiple escape routes to evade multiple drugs.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary dynamics of drug resistance.

claim: CDN analysis is crucial for stratifying patients for targeted therapy.
source: Moreover, CDN analysis is crucial for stratifying patients for targeted therapy, as only targeting genes that are positively selected during cancer evolution can truly achieve therapeutic effects.
evidence: This is a claim about the clinical utility of CDN analysis.

claim: A large database will facilitate the detection of negative selection which has eluded detection.
source: A large database will facilitate the detection of negative selection which has eluded detection (Chen et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications, supported by a citation.

claim: It will be possible to study the evolution of mutation mechanisms in cancer cells based on large samples.
source: It will also be possible to study the evolution of mutation mechanisms in cancer cells based on such large samples (Jackson and Loeb, 1998; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications, supported by citations.

claim: Cancers may be the first complex genetic system that can be unraveled thanks to massively repeated evolution.
source: Cancers may be the first such complex genetic systems that can be unraveled thanks to the massively repeated evolution.
evidence: This is a speculation about the unique opportunity cancer genomics provides.

claim: Single nucleotide variation (SNV) data for the TCGA cohort was downloaded from the GDC Data Portal.
source: Single nucleotide variation (SNV) data for the TCGA cohort was downloaded from the GDC Data Portal (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/, data version 2022-02-28).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about data sources.

claim: Only mutations identified by at least two pipelines were included in this study.
source: Only mutations identified by at least two pipelines were included in this study.
evidence: This is a methodological choice for data quality control.

claim: Mutations were filtered based on their population frequency recorded in gnomAD with an upper threshold of 1‰.
source: Mutations were further filtered based on their population frequency recorded in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD, version v2.1.1), with an upper threshold of 1‰.
evidence: This is a methodological choice for filtering germline variants.

claim: The study focused on coding region mutations of missense, nonsense, and synonymous types on autosomes.
source: We focused on coding region mutations of missense, nonsense, and synonymous types on autosomes.
evidence: This is a methodological choice about which mutations to analyze.

claim: Patients with a mutation load exceeding 3000 were identified as having a mutator phenotype and were excluded from the analysis.
source: Patients with a mutation load exceeding 3000 were identified as having a mutator phenotype and were excluded from our analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological choice for excluding hypermutated samples.

claim: In total, 7369 samples representing 12 cancer types were included for mutation analysis.
source: In total, 7369 samples representing 12 cancer types were included for mutation analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the final dataset used in the study.

claim: Fourfold degenerate sites are generally considered neutral, as any mutation path would not alter the encoded amino acid sequence.
source: In coding regions, fourfold degenerate sites are generally considered neutral, as any mutation path would not alter the encoded amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in molecular evolution.

claim: The study employed the deep learning framework Dig to calculate mutation rates.
source: Figure 3A shows the mutation rate landscape across all recurrence sites in breast, CNS and lung cancer using the deep learning framework Dig (Sherman et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the AI tool used, supported by a citation.

claim: There is no significant difference in mutation rate as a function of i detected by the Dig analysis.
source: While the mutation rate fluctuates around the average level, we detect no significant difference in mutation rate as a function of i (Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the AI-based mutation rate analysis.

claim: In CNS cancer, two sites exhibited exceptional mutability at i=6, surpassing the average by tenfold, and these are CpG sites corresponding to V774M and R222C in EGFR.
source: In CNS, two sites exhibited exceptional mutability at i=6, surpassing the average by tenfold. Unsurprisingly, these two are CpG sites and correspond to amino acid change of V774M and R222C in EGFR (Supplementary file 1), which are canonical actionable driver mutations in glioma target therapy.
evidence: This is a specific observation from the data analysis.

claim: The two highly mutable sites in CNS cancer called by AI appear to be selection driven.
source: In other words, the two sites called by AI for possible high mutability appear to be selection driven.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AI results in the context of known driver mutations.

claim: In the PAX3 gene example, the CDN site C1271T is estimated to have a twofold elevation in mutability.
source: This CDN site is estimated to have a twofold elevation in mutability, which is less than 1/50 of the necessary mutability to reach i≥3.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the detailed analysis of PAX3.

claim: The twofold elevation in mutability at the PAX3 CDN site is less than 1/50 of the necessary mutability to reach i≥3.
source: This CDN site is estimated to have a twofold elevation in mutability, which is less than 1/50 of the necessary mutability to reach i≥3.
evidence: This is a calculation showing that mutability alone cannot explain the recurrence.

claim: While AI often suggests sequence context to influence the local variation in mutation rate, the reported variation does not correspond to the distribution of CDNs.
source: Overall, while AI often suggests sequence context to influence the local variation in mutation rate, the reported variation does not correspond to the distribution of CDNs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the AI-based analysis.

claim: The α value (fold change between the most mutable motif and the average) increases from 4.7 to 8.8 and then to 11.5 for 3-mer, 5-mer, and 7-mer motifs respectively.
source: Since the number of motifs increases 16-fold between each length class, the α value increases from 4.7 to 8.8 and then to 11.5.
evidence: This is a finding from the motif analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The most mutable 7-mer, TAACGCG, which has a CpG site at the center, is only 11.52-fold higher than the average.
source: Nevertheless, even the most mutable 7-mer¸ TAACGCG, which has a CpG site at the center, is only 11.52-fold higher than the average.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the motif analysis.

claim: The 11.52-fold increase in mutability is insufficient to account for the high recurrences.
source: This spread is insufficient to account for the high recurrences, which decrease to ~0.002 for each increment of i (see PART II below).
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the observed mutability variation to the theoretical requirements.

claim: The high recurrence sites are not associated with the mutability of the motif.
source: The absence of a trend shows that the high recurrence sites are not associated with the mutability of the motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The sequences surrounding the high-recurrence sites appear rather random.
source: As can be seen in all 5 panels of Figure 4C, there are no outliers in the tail of the distribution. In other words, the sequences surrounding the high-recurrence sites appear rather random.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the consensus motif analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The analyses by the sequence approach do not find any association between high recurrence sites (i≥3) and the mutability of the local sequences.
source: In conclusion, the analyses by the sequence approach do not find any association between high recurrence sites (i≥3) and the mutability of the local sequences.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion from Part I of the study.

claim: Patients with recurrence sites do not bias toward high mutation loads.
source: The overall trend shows consistently that patients with recurrence sites do not bias toward high mutation loads.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of recurrence sites in patients with low mutation loads suggests that overall mutation burden is not a determining factor of recurrence.
source: The presence of recurrence sites in patients with low mutation loads suggests that overall mutation burden is not a determining factor of recurrence.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutation load analysis.

claim: In lung cancer, the signature compositions among patients with different recurrence cutoffs are statistically indistinguishable.
source: Figure 5B reveals that in lung cancer, the signature compositions among patients with different recurrence cutoffs are statistically indistinguishable (Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational signature analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Smoking (signature SBS4) consistently emerges as the predominant mutational process across all levels of recurrences in lung cancer.
source: Smoking (signature SBS4) consistently emerges as the predominant mutational process across all levels of recurrences.
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational signature analysis of lung cancer.

claim: In breast cancer, SBS2 and SBS13 exhibit some differences in the bins of i*=2 and i*=3, but the profiles remain rather constant for all bins of i*≥3.
source: In breast cancer, while SBS2 and SBS13 exhibit some differences in the bins of i*=2 and i*=3, the profiles remain rather constant for all bins of i*≥3.
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational signature analysis of breast cancer.

claim: In CNS cancer, SBS11 appears significantly different across bins, in particular, i≥20, and this is a signature associated with Temozolomide treatment.
source: In CNS cancer, SBS11 appears significantly different across bins, in particular, i≥20. This is a signature associated with Temozolomide treatment and should be considered a secondary effect.
evidence: This is a finding from the mutational signature analysis of CNS cancer with interpretation.

claim: While there are occasional differences in mutational signatures across i* bins, none of such differences can account for the recurrences.
source: In short, while there are occasional differences in mutational signatures across i* bins, none of such differences can account for the recurrences (see PART II).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutational signature analysis.

claim: The high-recurrence sites do not stand out for their mutation characteristics.
source: To conclude PART I, the high-recurrence sites do not stand out for their mutation characteristics.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion from Part I of the study.

claim: The variation in mutation rate across the whole genome can reasonably be approximated mathematically by a continuous distribution.
source: Therefore, the variation in mutation rate across the whole genome can reasonably be approximated mathematically by a continuous distribution, as will be done below.
evidence: This is a justification for the modeling approach based on the empirical findings.
